_provenance.run_mode: IN-SESSION REVIEW PASS, NOT AN EXTERNAL MODEL. The gemini CLI required by scripts/run-external-stages.mjs is not installed in this environment, so this stage was executed as a separate adversarial pass against engine/templates/stage2-preamble.txt rather than by an independent external reviewer. Independence is therefore WEAKER than on issues 2010 and 2011. Flagged for the operator at Phase 8.

geographic_flags.text: That was before the three London properties and the Sabah hotel were revalued.
geographic_flags.why: Two of the eight audited deals sit in East Malaysia (Grand Borneo Hotel in Sabah, and the Limbang company in Sarawak). Sarawak disappears entirely from the reader-facing text and Sabah survives only as the object 'the Sabah hotel'. London is named three times. The asset map is genuinely national; the copy reads Peninsular-and-London.
geographic_flags.fix: No change strictly required at this length, but if a card gains room, name Sarawak alongside Sabah rather than dropping it.

omission_flags.text: Malaysia audited Felda more closely than almost any agency it owns. What followed the audit was forbearance, and the settlers paid for it.
omission_flags.why: The view card asserts that settlers paid, but no card anywhere in the issue shows a settler-facing consequence. The reader is handed the emotional payoff without the evidence for it. This is the single largest structural weakness in the draft: an issue about an agency that exists for 112,000-odd settler families contains no settler-facing number and no settler voice. The brief itself flags that settler voice is thin across the whole source set.
omission_flags.fix: Ground the claim. The White Paper's own executive summary states that Felda's critical cash flow delayed Sara Hidup and Pendahuluan Hasil payments to settlers. That is a primary-sourced settler consequence and it belongs on a card, or the view must stop asserting it.

omission_flags.why: The provenance block says the record is deliberately bipartisan, and that is the strongest non-partisan asset the story has. But no reader-facing text carries it. A reader sees only 'the state audited, then did nothing' and will map that onto whichever government they already dislike. The bipartisanship is invisible where it matters.
omission_flags.fix: One clause establishing that the audit was commissioned by one government and the reopening runs under another would convert the issue from an anti-incumbent read to an anger-at-process read, which is the stated editorial anchor.

omission_flags.text: Ernst & Young found RM4.38 billion committed across the eight deals.
omission_flags.why: The issue never states what Ernst & Young actually concluded about conduct, only what it counted. A reader could finish the issue believing the audit found bad investments rather than governance failure.

cardinal_sin_flags.claim: Ernst & Young found RM4.38 billion committed across the eight deals. Roughly half of it, about RM2.2 billion, was already written off.
cardinal_sin_flags.why: The verified harshest accurate phrasing is not used. Ernst & Young's annex at 1.3.3 and 1.3.4 found governance failure, approvals without due diligence, and expressly 'elements of non-compliance and misconduct' (elemen ketidakpatuhan dan salah laku), including purchases made without or against board approval. The draft reduces all of that to an impairment number. Reporting only the money softens a finding the primary source states plainly.
cardinal_sin_flags.primary_source: Kertas Putih FELDA 2019, Lampiran 1, paras 1.3.3 and 1.3.4

cardinal_sin_flags.claim: What followed the audit was forbearance, and the settlers paid for it.
cardinal_sin_flags.why: Two problems. 'Forbearance' asserts deliberate refraining from enforcement, but the issue's own fact card records a criminal conviction and a RM2 billion civil suit, so the state did enforce, slowly and partially. And 'the settlers paid for it' asserts a causal transfer that no card evidences. As written the sentence claims more than the draft has shown.
cardinal_sin_flags.primary_source: Kertas Putih FELDA 2019, Ringkasan Eksekutif p.1 (settler payment delays); the draft's own fact card 1

cardinal_sin_flags.claim: MACC opened the Kensington file in 2017 and it is still open.
cardinal_sin_flags.why: This fuses two separately sourced facts into one asserted continuity. MACC's 2 September 2026 statement says an old investigation paper on the Park City Grand Plaza property has not been closed and is under mutual legal assistance; it does not date that paper to 2017. Separately, 2017 reporting says MACC opened papers on FIC's London and Kuching hotel purchases. The identification is a strong inference, not a stated fact, and the card presents it as stated.
cardinal_sin_flags.primary_source: MACC chief commissioner statement, 2 September 2026 (The Edge, FMT); Malay Mail 14 July 2017 and 3 August 2017

verification_log: Confirmed against the primary document that the Ernst & Young annex lists exactly eight projects at para 1.1.1 and that PT Eagle High Plantations is the only one absent from the MACC list of 2 September 2026. The central comparison holds.
Confirmed the RM4,382m and RM2,116m figures against Paparan 1 of the annex, and the 'roughly 50% of RM4.4 billion, reaching RM2.2 billion' wording against para 1.3.1.

Confirmed that no card names any person under investigation, and that the only named individual has a final conviction. The 3R posture is sound: no religious, royal or communal framing appears anywhere in the reader-facing text.

Ran the shoe test on party attribution. Because no party is named in any card, the copy reads identically whichever coalition made the deals. It passes, but see the MEDIUM omission flag: passing by silence costs the story its bipartisan anchor.
overall_assessment: Low measured bias, and the 3R and partisan discipline is genuinely strong: no party, community, religion or royal reference appears in reader-facing text, and the one named individual is named only because his conviction is final. The problems are not slant but proportion. First, an underclaim: the draft reports the money Ernst & Young counted and omits the conduct it found, which is the harsher and equally verified half. Second, an overclaim in the view card, which asserts both deliberate forbearance and settler harm, neither of which any card evidences, while the draft's own fact card shows partial enforcement. Third, a fused inference presented as fact on the Kensington file. Fourth, and most consequential editorially, the settlers are the subject of the closing sentence and are otherwise absent from the entire issue. Fixing the underclaim and grounding the settler claim in the White Paper's own account of delayed Sara Hidup payments would raise both accuracy and force at the same time.
